title: Low-Renin Hypertension: Aldosterone–Renin Ratio, Adrenal Vein Sampling, Liddle and AME
summary: Learn how the aldosterone-to-renin ratio screens for primary aldosteronism, why it must be read with aldosterone and confirmed, why adrenal vein sampling beats CT for choosing a side, and how Liddle syndrome and apparent mineralocorticoid excess give low renin with low aldosterone.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 25 Hit 5 (PAC/PRA screen and saline confirmation), Hit 13 (Liddle syndrome vs apparent mineralocorticoid excess) and Exam Trap 6 (imaging vs adrenal vein sampling). Checked against the 2023 Korean Endocrine Society consensus (Ha 2023), Romero 2016 (summary of the 2016 Endocrine Society guideline), Quencer 2021, Zhou 2020, Tetti 2018 and Lu 2022, all read as Europe PMC full text. The 2016 and 2025 Endocrine Society guidelines themselves are not open access in Europe PMC and were not read. Not taught: the reviewer’s “>50 virtually diagnostic” ARR level (no source read gives it; register flag rv-arr-50-diagnostic) and the “<3:1 = bilateral hyperplasia” AVS cut-off (sources read give lateralisation index ≥4 with cosyntropin, ≥2 without, and a grey zone; register flag rv-avs-li-cutoffs). The ARR minimum-PAC rule is taught with its caveat (register flag rv-arr-pac-minimum).

objectives: Calculate and interpret the aldosterone-to-renin ratio, including the role of aldosterone level and drug interference.
Explain why a positive screen needs confirmation and why adrenal vein sampling, not CT, decides unilateral disease.
Distinguish primary aldosteronism, Liddle syndrome and apparent mineralocorticoid excess from aldosterone, renin and supporting tests.

scenes.title: Three low-renin patients
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three adults with hypertension and low potassium, all with suppressed plasma renin. (1) Aldosterone 28 ng/dL, plasma renin activity 0.5 ng/mL/h, so the aldosterone-to-renin ratio is 56. (2) Aldosterone LOW as well as renin; the patient drinks licorice tea daily. (3) Primary aldosteronism already confirmed; CT shows a 1.2 cm left adrenal nodule. Question token: “Aldosterone, impostor, or which side?”

cues.text: Three patients with high blood pressure, low potassium and a suppressed renin. The first has an aldosterone of twenty-eight and a ratio of fifty-six.
The second has a low aldosterone too, and drinks licorice tea every day. The third has confirmed primary aldosteronism and a small nodule on CT.
Is aldosterone really the driver, is something else pressing the same switch, and which adrenal is to blame?

scenes.title: The renin–aldosterone loop
scenes.altText: Schematic loop. Renin leads to angiotensin II, which stimulates aldosterone from the zona glomerulosa (potassium and, less so, ACTH also stimulate it). Aldosterone binds the mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) in the kidney: sodium is reabsorbed through epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) and potassium is secreted. Guard card: 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (11β-HSD2) converts cortisol to inactive cortisone, because the MR binds cortisol and aldosterone with equal affinity in vitro. Result token: sodium retention and volume expansion suppress renin.

cues.text: Normally renin makes angiotensin two, which tells the zona glomerulosa to release aldosterone. Potassium, and to a lesser extent ACTH, also stimulate it.
Aldosterone binds the mineralocorticoid receptor in the kidney. Sodium is reabsorbed through epithelial sodium channels, and potassium is lost in the urine.
The receptor binds cortisol just as well as aldosterone in the test tube. An enzyme, eleven-beta-HSD2, guards it by turning cortisol into inactive cortisone.
When sodium is retained and volume expands, renin is switched off. So any disorder that over-drives this pathway gives hypertension with a low renin.

lines: Also K⁺, and less so ACTH

scenes.title: Three engines, one low renin
scenes.altText: Three engine cards. Primary aldosteronism (PA): autonomous aldosterone production, so aldosterone is high while renin is suppressed; hypokalemia is present in only a minority of patients. Apparent mineralocorticoid excess (AME): 11β-HSD2 deficiency (HSD11B2 mutations, autosomal recessive) or acquired inhibition by licorice or azole antifungals; cortisol activates the MR; in the classic form renin AND aldosterone are low and the urinary cortisol/cortisone ratio is high (the milder non-classic form can have normal aldosterone). Liddle syndrome: gain-of-function variants in ENaC subunit genes (SCNN1A, SCNN1B, SCNN1G), autosomal dominant; sodium is reabsorbed without aldosterone; renin is low and aldosterone is usually low. Tell-apart card: spironolactone helps AME but not Liddle; amiloride or triamterene (ENaC blockers) treat Liddle.

cues.text: Engine one is primary aldosteronism: the adrenal makes aldosterone on its own, so aldosterone is high while renin is suppressed. Low potassium is present in only a minority of patients, so a normal potassium does not exclude it.

Engine two is apparent mineralocorticoid excess. The 11-beta-HSD2 guard is missing or blocked, by an inherited defect or by licorice, so cortisol drives the receptor. In the classic form renin and aldosterone are both low.
Engine three is Liddle syndrome, an inherited gain-of-function in the epithelial sodium channel itself. The channel works without aldosterone, so renin is low and aldosterone is usually low too.

To tell the two low-aldosterone causes apart, apparent mineralocorticoid excess shows a high urinary cortisol to cortisone ratio and responds to spironolactone, while Liddle syndrome does not respond to spironolactone and is treated with amiloride or triamterene.

scenes.title: Screen, confirm, then lateralise
scenes.altText: Workflow cards. Screen: aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) = PAC (ng/dL) ÷ PRA (ng/mL/h); the most common positive cut-off is 30, and thresholds change with the renin assay and units. Read it with PAC: a high ratio with a low PAC can be an artefact of very low renin, so labs report PAC and renin with the ratio. Interference: β-blockers can give false-positive ratios; ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics and MR antagonists can give false negatives; correct hypokalemia first. Confirm: for example the saline infusion test (recumbent post-infusion PAC >10 ng/dL likely, <5 unlikely); confirmation may be skipped with spontaneous hypokalemia, renin below detection and PAC >20 ng/dL. Subtype: CT first to exclude a large mass; adrenal vein sampling (AVS) is the reference test; CT/MRI disagreed with AVS in 37.8% of 950 patients in a pooled analysis. AVS: a selectivity index (adrenal:peripheral cortisol) confirms cannulation; a lateralisation index (cortisol-corrected aldosterone, dominant ÷ non-dominant side) of 4 or more with cosyntropin indicates unilateral disease. Hook answers.

cues.text: Screen with the aldosterone-to-renin ratio: aldosterone in nanograms per decilitre divided by renin activity. The most common cut-off is thirty, but the threshold depends on the renin assay and the units.

Read the ratio with the aldosterone itself: a high ratio with a low aldosterone may only reflect a very low renin. Beta-blockers can push the ratio falsely up; diuretics and ACE inhibitors can push it falsely down. Correct low potassium first.

A positive screen needs a confirmatory test, such as saline infusion, unless low potassium is spontaneous, renin is undetectable and aldosterone is above twenty. Then CT, then adrenal vein sampling, because CT and sampling disagreed in about thirty-eight percent of patients in a pooled analysis.

Back to the hook. Patient one goes to confirmatory testing. Patient two is not primary aldosteronism: think licorice-induced mineralocorticoid excess. Patient three needs adrenal vein sampling before any surgery.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A ratio above 30 proves primary aldosteronism” (✓ read it with PAC and confirm with a suppression test); “Low renin plus hypertension means primary aldosteronism” (✓ if aldosterone is low too, think Liddle syndrome or apparent mineralocorticoid excess); “An adrenal nodule on CT is the adenoma” (✓ CT can mislead; adrenal vein sampling decides side before surgery).

cues.text: Trap one: a ratio above thirty proves primary aldosteronism. No: read it with the aldosterone level, and confirm with a suppression test.
Trap two: low renin with hypertension means primary aldosteronism. No: if aldosterone is low too, think Liddle syndrome or apparent mineralocorticoid excess.
Trap three: the nodule on CT is the adenoma. No: nodules can be non-functioning, so adrenal vein sampling decides the side before surgery.

props.title: ✗ “Low renin = primary aldosteronism.”
lines: ✓ Low aldosterone too → Liddle or AME

props.title: ✗ “CT nodule = the adenoma.”
lines: ✓ Adrenal vein sampling decides the side

scenes.title: Driver, impostor, stuck pedal
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “The sodium accelerator is floored in all three, so renin always hits the brakes. Primary aldosteronism = the real DRIVER (aldosterone) floors it. AME = an IMPOSTOR (cortisol) slips into the seat because the guard (11β-HSD2) is off duty, or bribed by licorice. Liddle = a STUCK PEDAL (ENaC): nobody needs to press it, and spironolactone cannot lift it.” Tokens: driver = aldosterone high · impostor = cortisol · stuck pedal = ENaC. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: the sodium accelerator is floored in all three, so renin always brakes. In primary aldosteronism the real driver, aldosterone, floors it. In mineralocorticoid excess an impostor, cortisol, takes the seat because the guard is off duty. In Liddle syndrome the pedal is stuck, and spironolactone cannot lift it.

Where it breaks: aldosterone in primary aldosteronism is not always strikingly high; cut-offs depend on the assay; and Liddle syndrome and mineralocorticoid excess vary, with some patients having normal potassium or only mild hypertension.

props.title: Where it breaks

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Low renin + HIGH aldosterone → primary aldosteronism → confirm → CT → adrenal vein sampling”, “Low renin + LOW aldosterone → Liddle (ENaC) or AME (11β-HSD2, licorice)”.

cues.text: In low-renin hypertension read the aldosterone first, because a high autonomous aldosterone points to primary aldosteronism that still needs confirmation and adrenal vein sampling, while a low aldosterone points to Liddle syndrome or apparent mineralocorticoid excess.

props.label: Renin low + aldosterone HIGH → PA → confirm → CT → AVS
Renin low + aldosterone LOW → Liddle (ENaC) or AME (11β-HSD2)

explanation.what: Plain language: several conditions push the kidney to hold sodium and lose potassium, which raises blood pressure and switches renin off. In primary aldosteronism the adrenal over-makes aldosterone; in two rare mimics the receptor or the sodium channel is driven without aldosterone. Scientific terms: primary aldosteronism (PA), aldosterone-producing adenoma, bilateral idiopathic hyperplasia, plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC), plasma renin activity (PRA), direct renin concentration, aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR), saline infusion test, adrenal vein sampling (AVS), selectivity and lateralisation indices, mineralocorticoid receptor (MR), epithelial sodium channel (ENaC), 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (11β-HSD2), Liddle syndrome, apparent mineralocorticoid excess (AME).
explanation.why: Aldosterone acting on the MR increases sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion; the resulting volume expansion suppresses renin. In PA aldosterone is autonomous, so the ratio rises. In AME cortisol reaches the MR because 11β-HSD2 is deficient or inhibited (licorice, azoles); in Liddle syndrome ENaC is overactive without aldosterone; both suppress renin and usually aldosterone (non-classic AME can have normal aldosterone).
explanation.measure: ARR = PAC (ng/dL) ÷ PRA (ng/mL/h); the most common positive cut-off is 30, and equivalent thresholds differ by renin assay and unit. Interpret with PAC; a high ARR with low PAC may reflect very low renin. β-blockers, central α2-agonists and NSAIDs tend toward false positives; ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics and MR antagonists toward false negatives; correct hypokalemia. Confirm (for example saline infusion: recumbent post-infusion PAC >10 ng/dL likely, 5–10 intermediate, <5 unlikely), unless spontaneous hypokalemia, renin below detection and PAC >20 ng/dL. Subtype: CT first, then AVS; lateralisation index ≥4 with cosyntropin (Endocrine Society: >2 unstimulated). AME: high urinary cortisol/cortisone (or THF + allo-THF/THE) ratio. Liddle: genetic testing of SCNN1A/B/G.
explanation.differs: PA (aldosterone high, renin low; MR antagonist works) vs AME (aldosterone low, renin low; high cortisol/cortisone ratio; MR antagonist works) vs Liddle (aldosterone low, renin low; spironolactone fails, amiloride or triamterene works). CT (anatomy; incidental non-functioning adenomas) vs AVS (function, side of aldosterone excess).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: calculate an ARR and choose the next step; spot a drug that causes a false-positive or false-negative ARR; pick Liddle or AME from low renin plus low aldosterone with a licorice or family history clue; choose AVS over CT before adrenalectomy.

points: Receptor or channel driven without aldosterone

mnemonic.text: The sodium accelerator is floored in all three, so renin always brakes. Primary aldosteronism = the real DRIVER (aldosterone). AME = an IMPOSTOR (cortisol) in the seat because the guard (11β-HSD2) is off duty or bribed by licorice. Liddle = a STUCK PEDAL (ENaC) that spironolactone cannot lift.
mnemonic.explanation: Separates high-aldosterone from low-aldosterone causes of low-renin hypertension and links each to its discriminating test or drug response.
mnemonic.limitation: PAC in primary aldosteronism is not always strikingly high; ratio cut-offs are assay-dependent; Liddle syndrome and AME vary in severity, with some patients normokalemic or only mildly hypertensive.

The car analogy ignores other causes of low-renin hypertension not covered here.
takeaway: In low-renin hypertension read the aldosterone first, because a high autonomous aldosterone points to primary aldosteronism that still needs confirmation and adrenal vein sampling, while a low aldosterone points to Liddle syndrome or apparent mineralocorticoid excess.

questions.stem: A hypertensive adult on no interfering drugs has potassium 3.2 mmol/L, plasma aldosterone 28 ng/dL and plasma renin activity 0.5 ng/mL/h (detectable). What is the best next step?

options.text: Perform a confirmatory test such as saline infusion
options.rationale: Correct. The ratio is 56 with a raised aldosterone, a positive screen; renin is detectable, so the criteria for skipping confirmation are not met.

options.text: Proceed to adrenalectomy if CT shows a nodule
options.rationale: Incorrect. Primary aldosteronism is not yet confirmed, and CT alone does not establish which side is secreting.

options.text: Report a normal ratio; no further work-up
options.rationale: Incorrect. A ratio of 56 exceeds the commonly used cut-off of 30.

options.text: Repeat the ratio after starting a β-blocker
options.rationale: Incorrect. β-blockers suppress renin and can cause false-positive ratios.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old with severe hypertension, hypokalemia, suppressed renin and low aldosterone does not improve on spironolactone but normalises on amiloride. His father had the same findings. Most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Correct. ENaC gain-of-function, autosomal dominant, low renin and aldosterone, unresponsive to spironolactone and treated with ENaC blockers.
Incorrect. AME is driven through the MR, so spironolactone helps; inherited AME is autosomal recessive.
Incorrect. Aldosterone would be high, not low.
Incorrect. Renal artery narrowing stimulates renin, so renin is not suppressed.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old with confirmed primary aldosteronism has a 1.2 cm left adrenal nodule on CT. Cosyntropin-stimulated adrenal vein sampling is adequately selective on both sides, with a lateralisation index of 1.6. Best interpretation?

options.text: No lateralisation: manage as bilateral disease, typically with an MR antagonist
options.rationale: Correct. An index well below 4 does not show a unilateral source; the nodule may be non-functioning.

options.text: Left aldosterone-producing adenoma: proceed to left adrenalectomy
options.rationale: Incorrect. CT shows anatomy, not secretion; CT and AVS frequently disagree.

options.text: The sampling failed because the index is low
options.rationale: Incorrect. Cannulation success is judged by the selectivity index (adrenal vs peripheral cortisol), which was adequate.
Incorrect. An index of 1.6 does not lateralise to either side.

claims.text: Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone regulation; MR action on sodium and potassium; volume expansion suppresses renin; 11β-HSD2 protects the MR from cortisol.
Hypokalemia is present in only a minority of patients with PA.
ARR = PAC/PRA; common cut-off 30; thresholds assay/unit-dependent; read with PAC; drug interferences; correct hypokalemia.
Confirmatory testing required; saline infusion cut-offs; confirmation may be skipped with spontaneous hypokalemia, undetectable renin and PAC >20 ng/dL.

CT first, AVS as reference; CT/MRI–AVS discordance 37.8% (950 patients); selectivity index for cannulation; lateralisation index ≥4 with cosyntropin; unilateral → adrenalectomy, bilateral → MR antagonist.
claims.note: The 37.8% figure is from Kempers 2009 as reported by Ha 2023 and Quencer 2021; the original was not read.

claims.text: Liddle syndrome: autosomal dominant ENaC gain-of-function; low renin and usually low aldosterone; spironolactone ineffective; amiloride/triamterene effective.
claims.note: Tetti 2018 systematic review: hypoaldosteronemia (<5 ng/dL) in 58.2% and hypokalemia in 71.8% of reported cases.

claims.text: AME: 11β-HSD2 deficiency (autosomal recessive) or licorice/azole inhibition; low renin and (in the classic form) low aldosterone; high urinary cortisol/cortisone ratio; MR antagonists effective.
claims.note: Lu 2022 Table 2: non-classic AME has normal aldosterone and only slightly increased urinary cortisol/cortisone.

claims.text: Reviewer: PAC/PRA >50 “virtually diagnostic”; AVS ratio “<3:1 = bilateral hyperplasia”; oral sodium loading details.
claims.note: Not taught. No source read gives >50 as virtually diagnostic (Ha 2023 says specificity rises with ARR, and confirmation is skipped only with spontaneous hypokalemia, undetectable renin and PAC >20). Sources read give LI ≥4 stimulated (≥2 unstimulated) and a grey zone, not a <3 bilateral cut-off. Oral sodium loading is listed by Ha 2023 but not taught in detail here.

claims.text: Scenario invented; loop and kidney cell schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 25 Hit 5 calls a PAC/PRA ratio >50 “virtually diagnostic”. No source read gives this level: Ha 2023 says specificity rises as the ratio rises, and Ha 2023 and Romero 2016 allow skipping confirmation only with spontaneous hypokalemia, renin below detection and PAC >20 ng/dL. The lesson teaches confirmation after a positive screen (register flag rv-arr-50-diagnostic).

Ch. 25 Hit 5 says the ratio counts “only if PAC itself is elevated too”. Romero 2016 (2016 Endocrine Society guideline) says to interpret the ratio with PAC, but Ha 2023 notes that 30–40% of ratio-positive PA patients have PAC <15 ng/dL, and ratio cut-offs vary with renin assay and units. The lesson teaches “read with PAC” without a fixed minimum (register flag rv-arr-pac-minimum).

Ch. 25 Exam Trap 6 gives AVS ratios of >4:1 = adenoma and <3:1 = bilateral hyperplasia. Sources read give a lateralisation index of 4 with cosyntropin (Ha 2023 Table 7: ≥4 with, ≥2 without; the 2016 Endocrine Society guideline as tabulated by Quencer 2021: >4 with, >2 without; Ha 2023 text recommends 4 under both conditions), note a grey zone and centre-to-centre variation, and describe unilateral disease (adenoma or unilateral hyperplasia) rather than “adenoma” only; no source read gives <3 as the bilateral cut-off (register flag rv-avs-li-cutoffs).
